extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent applicants, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent claim subject-matter eligibility under the USPTO 2019 Patent Eligibility Guidance (PEG), focusing on Step 2A (Prong One and Prong Two), Step 2B, the considerations that indicate integration of judicial exceptions into practical applications, and the examiner's prima facie burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of a judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the considerations identified by the Supreme Court and the Federal Circuit to ensure that the claim as a whole “integrates [the] judicial exception into a practical application [that] will apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the judicial exception.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The considerations (e.g., improving technology, effecting a particular treatment or prophylaxis, implementing with a particular machine, particular transformation, etc.) in MPEP 2106.05(a)-(c) and 2106.05(e)-(h) should be used. A specific way of achieving a result is not a stand-alone consideration, but the specificity of claim limitations is relevant to several considerations. If, upon evaluation of these considerations, the additional limitations impose a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, the claim is eligible at Step 2A. Example: SRI International v. Cisco — improvements to computer network technology (network monitors analyzing traffic) constituted integration and eligibility at Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement in the functioning of a computer or other technology/technical field
rubrics_metrics.description: An important consideration is whether the claimed invention improves the functioning of a computer or other technology or technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should evaluate the specification to determine if the disclosure provides sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. The specification need not explicitly state the improvement but must describe the invention so the improvement would be apparent to a person of ordinary skill. If the specification asserts an improvement in a conclusory manner (bare assertion without necessary detail), the examiner should not find the claim improves technology. The claim must be evaluated to ensure it reflects the disclosed improvement (it need not recite the improvement in words like “thereby increasing the bandwidth”). Under the 2019 PEG, the Step 2A “improvements” analysis determines whether the claim pertains to an improvement to the functioning of a computer or other technology without reference to whether it is well-understood, routine, or conventional. Consideration applies equally across technologies (computer-implemented, life sciences, etc.). Examiners are generally not expected to make qualitative judgments on the merits of the asserted improvement; if the examiner concludes no improvement, the burden shifts to applicant to provide persuasive evidence (e.g., 37 C.F.R. § 1.132 declaration) showing what the specification conveys to one of ordinary skill. Examples cited: CellzDirect, Rapid Litigation Management, Finjan, Diehr, Trading Technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying/using a judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim can integrate a judicial exception into a practical application by applying or using the judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration covers applying abstract ideas, laws of nature, or natural phenomena to effect treatments (e.g., acupuncture, administration of medication, dialysis, transplants, phototherapy, physiotherapy, radiation therapy, surgery). In assessing this consideration, evaluate the particularity of the treatment, whether the treatment has more than a nominal relationship to the exception, and whether the limitation is merely extra-solution activity or a field-of-use. Examples include Classen Immunotherapies, Vanda, and vaccination/genotype administration scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity of the treatment or prophylaxis limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must be “particular,” i.e., specifically identified so that it does not encompass all applications of the judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the administration step is specific (e.g., administering a lower-than-normal dosage of a beta blocker to patients with a specific genotype), it can integrate a mental-process exception into a practical application. By contrast, a generic administration step such as “administering a suitable medication” is not particular and does not integrate the exception. Use concrete claim language to determine particularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the limitation has more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment/prophylaxis limitation must have more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the recited judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim reciting treating blood glucose >250 mg/dl with insulin has a meaningful connection to the law of nature (treats ketoacidosis risk) and integrates the exception; treating such a patient with aspirin (not known to treat ketoacidosis) has at best a nominal connection and does not integrate the law of nature. Evaluate whether the claimed treatment meaningfully applies the recited exception to address the identified condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the limitation is merely extra-solution activity or a field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must impose meaningful limits on the judicial exception and cannot be merely extra-solution activity or a field-of-use restriction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Steps that only administer vaccines to gather data for a later mental-analysis step are extra-solution activity and do not integrate the exception. However, a subsequent step that applies the analyzed information (e.g., vaccinating a second group according to a newly determined lowest-risk schedule) applies the exception and integrates it into a practical application. Determine whether the claimed limitation does more than serve as a necessary precursor for using the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementing the judicial exception with a particular machine or manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing the judicial exception with a particular machine or manufacture is a consideration that may indicate integration into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MPEP 2106.05(b) and associated examples to evaluate whether recitation of a particular machine or manufacture meaningfully integrates the exception. Generic computer components (e.g., “data processing system,” “communications controller”) may be insufficient; assess specificity and how the machine interacts with the exception. See CLS Bank and related examples where generic computer elements were merely instructions to implement the abstract idea on a computer and did not indicate integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effecting a particular transformation or reduction of an article
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations that effect a particular transformation or reduction of an article are considerations that may indicate integration into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed steps change the state or identity of an article in a way that meaningfully limits the judicial exception per MPEP guidance and examples. Use cited examples in the PEG for analogous fact patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other meaningful ways of applying the judicial exception / negative indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the judicial exception in some other meaningful way may indicate integration; conversely, certain features generally do not indicate integration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considerations that may indicate integration include particular machines, transformations, and treatment applications. Considerations that may not indicate integration include merely reciting the words “apply it” (or an equivalent), adding extra-solution activity, or generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment. See MPEP 2106.05(b)-2106.05(h) for examples. The 2019 PEG preserved many prior considerations except changes to the improvements analysis and extra-solution activity treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of claim limitations (relevance to evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specificity of claim limitations is relevant to the evaluation of many considerations (e.g., use of a particular machine, particular transformation, whether limitations are mere instructions to apply an exception), though specificity alone is not a stand-alone consideration in Step 2A Prong Two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how specifically the claim limitations describe the implementation, machine, transformation, or steps. Specific, detailed limitations that reflect an asserted improvement or particular application are more likely to integrate an exception than vague or generic recitations. The specification may make the improvement apparent even if the claim does not use explicit ‘improvement’ language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claim as a whole (evaluate limitations together)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong Two analysis considers the claim as a whole: the judicial-exception-containing limitations and the additional elements must be evaluated together to determine whether the claim integrates the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not evaluate additional limitations in isolation or in a vacuum; examine how limitations interact and impact each other. Example: Bascom — filtering installed at an ISP server remote from end-users with customizable filtering features, considered together with other limitations, produced an improvement in technology. The analysis should address the combined effect of limitations on integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra-solution activity analysis: Step 2A vs Step 2B (conventionality consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a limitation is extra-solution activity is considered differently at Step 2A versus Step 2B: well-understood, routine, conventional activity is not a consideration at Step 2A under the 2019 PEG.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP 2106.05(g) previously explained that whether a limitation is well-known is a factor in extra-solution activity determinations at Step 2B. Under the 2019 PEG, well-understood, routine, conventional activity will only be considered if the analysis proceeds to Step 2B. Thus, at Step 2A, whether a limitation is extra-solution activity should not be based on whether it is well-known. For examples of extra-solution activity that are unconventional, see Example 45 (Controller for Injection Mold).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a prima facie case of subject-matter ineligibility (examiner burden)
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner bears the initial burden to establish a prima facie case of ineligibility by explaining why a claim is ineligible clearly and specifically so the applicant has sufficient notice and can effectively respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When practicable, examiners should indicate how subject-matter eligibility rejections might be overcome. A Step 2B rejection should: (1) identify the judicial exception recited in the claim and explain why it is considered an exception (Step 2A Prong One); (2) for abstract ideas, explain why a specific limitation falls within one of the enumerated groupings (mathematical concepts, mental processes, certain methods of organizing human activity) or use the 2019 PEG 'tentative abstract idea' procedure; (3) for laws of nature/natural phenomena, identify the law/phenomenon recited and explain why; (4) evaluate and explain why additional elements individually and in combination do not integrate the exception into a practical application using the 2019 PEG considerations (Step 2A Prong Two); and (5) explain why the additional elements do not result in significantly more at Step 2B. If the examiner concludes certain elements are well-understood, routine, conventional, the examiner must expressly support the rejection with one of the four options specified in the Berkheimer Memorandum. Once the examiner satisfies the initial burden, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut with argument or evidence (37 C.F.R. § 1.132); examiners must carefully consider all applicant arguments and evidence and provide a rebuttal in the next Office action if maintaining the rejection. See MPEP § 2106.07 for formulation guidance and MPEP 716.01 and 37 C.F.R. § 1.132 for evidence submission procedures.
